Compared the exact target against the proved scope and separately assessed the draft's PARTIAL resolution label.
Reproved the incidence-gadget reduction to perfect matching, both cycle-splicing bounds, every nil certificate, all radius inequalities, and the conditional sublinear-factor implication.
Checked the complete-bipartite distance calculation and the Hamiltonian graph containing an n/3-component triangle factor.

Ran an exact integer/rational checker over all 33,867 simple graphs with 1 through 6 vertices for the applicable implications and splice constructions; checked the matching gadget through 4 vertices, 3,446 cyclic bipartition patterns, and nine triangle-family instances. claims.claim: Existence of a 2-factor, and an explicit 2-factor when one exists, can be determined in polynomial time.
claims.evidence: At a degree-d vertex, every perfect matching in the auxiliary graph matches its d−2 private dummies to distinct incidence vertices, leaving exactly two incidences to be matched through original-edge links. Those links therefore form a spanning degree-2 subgraph. Conversely, a 2-factor matches its selected incidences through edge links and permits a bijection between the remaining d−2 incidences and dummies. The auxiliary graph has polynomial size and an explicit perfect matching recovers the factor; vertices of degree below two are correctly rejected.
claims.search_method: Direct bijection proof between 2-factors and auxiliary perfect matchings, supplemented by exhaustive exact checking of every graph through four vertices.

claims.claim: If the 2-factor routine reports that none exists, returning (G,nil) is correct.
claims.evidence: A Hamiltonian cycle is itself a spanning 2-regular subgraph. Thus a graph without a 2-factor cannot be Hamiltonian, and distance zero makes (G,nil) a valid Sidestep output. The checker also confirmed this implication for every simple graph through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Direct necessary-condition proof plus exhaustive exact small-graph enumeration.

claims.claim: If G has a 2-factor with q cycle components, one can add at most q edges and explicitly obtain a Hamiltonian cycle; if G is connected, at most q−1 additions suffice.
claims.evidence: Breaking one witness edge in each factor cycle and cyclically joining the resulting q paths uses at most q absent connector edges; the broken edges remain in the returned graph but are omitted from the witness. When G is connected, an original edge from the current merged cycle to an unmerged factor cycle exists. Removing one witness edge incident to each endpoint and adding the second cross-edge merges the cycles while requiring at most one new graph edge. Repeating q−1 times proves the stronger bound.
claims.search_method: Constructive splice proof, with both constructions executed exhaustively on all applicable graphs through six vertices.

claims.claim: For every fixed real 0<c≤3, Sidestep(Hamiltonian Cycle,dist_e,n/c) is in FP.
claims.evidence: Disconnected graphs and graphs without a 2-factor have correct distance-zero nil outputs. Otherwise, a connected 2-factor has q≤n/3 components because every simple cycle has at least three vertices, and the connected splice adds at most q−1≤n/3≤n/c edges. The matching and splice operations are polynomial, preserve the labeled vertex set, and explicitly return the Hamiltonian cycle; finitely many n<3 cases can be decided directly.
claims.search_method: Full branch and radius audit, supplemented by exhaustive exact checking through six vertices.

claims.claim: For arbitrary fixed c>0, the target is polynomially solvable on graphs whose girth is at least c.
claims.evidence: Under the promise that G has girth g≥c, every cycle of any 2-factor has at least g vertices, so qg≤n and q≤n/c. Connectivity and factor failure give correct nil branches; otherwise the splice uses at most q−1≤n/c additions. Acyclic promised graphs fall into the no-2-factor branch. The checker computed girths with integer arithmetic and confirmed the bound on every applicable graph through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Promise-condition proof using factor-cycle lengths, plus exhaustive exact girth and splice checks.

claims.claim: A general cheap non-Hamiltonicity edit is obtained from a component-count obstruction.
claims.evidence: Given the stated S and partition, deleting all cross-part edges makes H−S have at least p components. If S is nonempty, deleting |S| vertices from a Hamiltonian cycle leaves at most |S| nonempty path components; if S is empty, a Hamiltonian graph is connected. Hence p>max{1,|S|} certifies non-Hamiltonicity. When the specified deletions number at most n/c, they give the claimed valid edit and can be performed polynomially.
claims.search_method: Direct component-count obstruction proof; the checker exhaustively verified the Hamiltonian component inequality through six vertices.

claims.claim: For every c, any graph with a vertex of degree at most n/c admits a polynomial-time valid nil output within radius n/c.
claims.evidence: Deleting precisely the edges incident with such a vertex costs deg(v)≤n/c and isolates it. For n≥2 the resulting graph cannot contain a spanning cycle; the remaining finite small convention is directly decidable. Degrees and the edit are computable in polynomial time. Exact rational tests over several c values and every graph through six vertices found no exception.
claims.search_method: Direct isolation construction plus exhaustive integer/rational small-instance checks.

claims.claim: A sublinear-component 2-factor routine would settle the full target for every fixed c.
claims.evidence: If b(n)=o(n), then for fixed c there is a constant N with b(n)−1≤n/c for every n≥N. First reject disconnected and no-2-factor graphs correctly. On a connected graph, splice when q−1≤n/c; if q−1>n/c, the routine's guarantee implies contrapositively that G is not Hamiltonian, so (G,nil) is correct. Inputs below N can be solved exactly in constant work relative to the fixed c. This proves the conditional implication without assuming that such a routine currently exists.
claims.search_method: Direct audit of the asymptotic quantifiers, connectivity branch, and contrapositive; finite checking is inapplicable to the hypothetical o(n) premise.

claims.claim: For every c>3, high minimum degree alone cannot guarantee a Hamiltonian graph within n/c edits.
claims.evidence: For c>3 the interval 1/c<α<(1−1/c)/2 is nonempty and contains a rational α. For multiples n of its denominator, K_{a,b} with a=αn<b has minimum degree a>n/c. In any cyclic ordering, if x and z count B-B and A-A adjacencies, incidence counting gives x−z=b−a, so every Hamiltonian supergraph requires at least b−a additions. Alternating the a vertices with a nonempty B-blocks realizes a cycle after exactly b−a additions. Thus the edit distance is b−a=(1−2α)n>n/c.
claims.search_method: Exact cyclic-incidence proof, checked over 3,446 bipartition patterns and rational parameter choices without floating point.

claims.claim: The n/3 component bound for an arbitrary 2-factor remains tight even under the promise that the graph is Hamiltonian.
claims.evidence: For n=3q, partition the vertices into q triples and include each triple's triangle. Ordering the vertices layer-by-layer across the triples makes consecutive vertices, including the wraparound pair, belong to different triples when q≥2. Adding those ordering edges gives a Hamiltonian cycle while the original q triangles remain a 2-factor with q=n/3 components. The construction was checked exactly for q=2 through 10.
claims.search_method: Explicit infinite-family construction plus exact verification of nine representative family members.

target_evidence: The exact target demands an unconditional polynomial-time Sidestep algorithm, or a disproof, for every fixed c>0 and every input graph. The draft rigorously proves the complete c≤3 case and several additional promised or conditional cases, which is material progress. It does not resolve arbitrary graphs for c>3: the girth result is only a promise result, the sublinear-component routine is hypothetical, and the complete-bipartite family is explicitly only a barrier to one proof method because those graphs already admit a distance-zero nil output. The final writeup clearly states that the universal c>3 case remains unresolved, so it does not overclaim target coverage. Accordingly target coverage is VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS, and the draft's claimed_resolution of PARTIAL is ACCURATE.
